    Bagging & Random Forests

    From one email to a forest

    Should a dollar sign send an email to spam? Start with real labeled emails, see how a tree learns its questions, and test whether several trees make better predictions together.

    1. Ensemble modelsHear two trees answer the same question and see four ways to combine models.
    2. Bagging and Random Forest intuitionDraw training rows, trace the trees, and see why averaging can steady a prediction.
    3. Random Forest implementationUse the full Spambase dataset to compare models and read their tuning curves.
    4. Randomized SearchCompare a full grid with a fixed search budget on the same folds.
    5. Out-of-bag pointsScore an email using only the trees that left it out of training.
    6. Interview questionsExplain feature importance, bias and variance, and when a branch earns its place.

    Would you send this to spam?

    “Your invoice is ready. Total due $80.” Would you classify it as Spam just because it contains a dollar sign?

    Test a one-clue rule against labeled examples

    Try this rule. Send any email containing $ to Spam. The invoice above is made up. The two emails below are actual records with labels we can check.

    A decision tree also follows rules. During training, it learns which questions to ask, where to put the cutoffs, and when a follow-up question helps separate the recorded labels.

    One email to classify

    We train on samples from 12 past emails with recorded labels. Both trees get a separate email, , with the same two measurements, or features. We keep its label hidden while they predict Legitimate or Spam.

    Dollar signs ($) ·

    Count the $ characters, divide by the total characters, and multiply by 100. One $ in 1,000 characters gives 0.1%.

    Exclamation marks (!) ·

    Count the ! characters the same way. For example, 3 exclamation marks in 800 characters gives 3 ÷ 800 × 100 = 0.375%.

    The 3-in-800 calculation is an illustration. The dataset supplies measured percentages and labels for 4,601 emails. An ID such as E574 identifies the row in the data file. UCI Spambase

    Four ways to combine models

    Follow , the same email we just traced. Bagging shows our two fitted trees. The other diagrams illustrate how each method would handle the email.

    Bagging

    Train each tree separately on its own sample of past emails.

    Boosting

    In gradient boosting, each new tree learns a correction to the current model.

    Stacking

    Train a separate model to combine the scores from other models.

    Cascading

    Run a quick filter first. How sure it is determines where the email goes next.

    Where did the cutoffs come from?

    The tree compares possible cuts by how well they separate the recorded labels. A new draw changes which values and labels are available at each node.

    How does stacking get training examples?

    Picture the 12 past emails divided into three groups of four. Each group is a fold. In each round, both base models train on two folds and predict for the third.

    After all three rounds, train the combiner. Pool the score rows from A, B, and C. You now have 12 rows, each with the decision tree’s score, the logistic model’s score, and the email’s ground-truth label.

    These are out-of-fold predictions because each email’s scores come from models trained on the other folds. The final test set stays separate.

    Draw a training sample

    Bagging

    Draw a bootstrap sample

    The two trees disagreed because their training samples gave them different evidence. We can make different samples from the same 12 labeled email records.

    Bootstrap · Draw a training set

    Make 12 draws. Every row stays eligible after each draw, so the tray may contain multiple copies of an email and leave other emails out. That tray is one bootstrap sample.

    Aggregate · Combine the predictions

    Fit one tree per tray. All the trees classify the same held-out email. You can count their class votes or average their predicted probabilities.

    Bagging is short for bootstrap aggregating. Draw a new sample and fit a model for each tray, then combine the models’ predictions.

      Quiz 2

      1. Draw the whole row. Each ticket keeps its two features and recorded label together.

      Check your count for Tree 1
      What changes without replacement?

      With 12 draws from 12 original rows and no replacement, every row appears once. Drawing fewer than 12 without replacement gives a subset. With replacement, repeated and omitted rows can occur even when the number of draws equals the number of original rows.

      Now fit a tree on each tray. The third tree gives us another prediction for the email that the first two disagreed on.

      Random Forest intuition

      Train three trees and combine their answers

      Let each tree learn from its own tray. Then give all three the same held-out email from the opening and follow the questions down each tree.

      These three trees demonstrate bagging. Both features are available at every split. The next chapter adds the per-split feature sampling that distinguishes a Random Forest.

      1. Sample. Draw 12 rows with replacement for each tree.
      2. Fit. Use the measured features and recorded labels to choose splits that make the child groups less mixed.
      3. Predict. Pass the same two input values down each tree until they reach a leaf.
      4. Combine. Count class votes or average the leaf probabilities for Spam.

      Run the core code

      Change how the training rows are drawn, fit one tree, and predict the same email. Then run the cell that fits all three trees.

      Open intuition notebook

      X holds the 12 rows’ dollar-sign and exclamation-mark frequencies. y holds their labels, encoded as 0 for Legitimate and 1 for Spam. email holds the same two feature values for our held-out email.

      draw = demo_draws[0]
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion='gini', max_depth=2, random_state=0)
tree.fit(X.loc[draw], y.loc[draw])
tree.predict(email)
      Walk through the code line by line
      1. Replay the draw IDs. demo_draws[0] stores the first tray you just saw. These saved samples were selected to make differences between trees easy to inspect.
      2. Set up the tree. Gini measures how mixed the labels are. Depth 2 allows two questions along a path. The tree seed controls random choices during fitting.
      3. Fit the tree. Use the same loc[draw] IDs in X and y so repeated rows keep their own labels.
      4. Predict. tree.predict(email) follows the questions for the held-out email and reports its predicted class.

      To draw a fresh tray, set rng = np.random.default_rng(11) and try draw = rng.choice(X.index, size=len(X), replace=True). Change replace to False and compare how many distinct rows you get.

      Expected output and what to point at

      Read the sample IDs first, then the predicted class. The implementation notebook uses the full dataset and adds per-split feature sampling.

      Compare the measurement with each cutoff. Follow the highlighted branch to the leaf and read the label counts.

      Quiz 3

      Work through the three paths and the two aggregation rules
      Is vote share the same as average predicted probability?

      Each hard vote contributes one class. In a probability average, a leaf with two Spam rows and one Legitimate row contributes a Spam probability of 2/3. For example, leaf probabilities of 0.49, 0.49 and 0.99 give two Legitimate hard votes, while the mean Spam probability of about 0.657 predicts Spam. Scikit-learn’s Random Forest classifier picks the class with the largest mean probability.

      Scikit-learn probability reference

      How would an ensemble predict a number?

      Suppose three regression trees estimate minutes until an email gets a reply. Train them on a different dataset containing actual reply times. For one email they might predict 9, 11 and 13 minutes. Their mean is (9 + 11 + 13) ÷ 3 = 11 minutes. These times illustrate regression. The Spambase rows supply class labels.

      Scikit-learn regression prediction reference

      Sampling rows gave us different trees. What happens if we also vary the features each node is allowed to consider?

      How do we get different trees?

      Draw rows for trees and features for splits

      If every tree can consider dollar signs at every split, several trees might lean on the same clue. A Random Forest draws a candidate set of features at each node. This gives other clues a chance to shape the tree.

      1. Which emails does this tree learn from? The bootstrap draw picks rows for the whole tree. Each copy of a row adds one count to its class.
      2. Which features can this node use? A feature draw chooses candidate columns. The draw at the next node is fresh.
      3. What is the best available split? Among its candidates, the tree picks the question that most reduces weighted Gini impurity for the rows at that node.

      Change the candidate features at each node

      Keep Tree 2’s 12 training draws fixed and replay different candidate draws. The root sends its rows to the Yes or No child. A mixed child tries cutoffs on its own list of candidates.

      Quiz 4

      Try it. Read the root’s question with Both features. Click Reveal next feature draw and compare the new question and child rows. Advance again to see a fresh set of candidates.

      Work through the first Gini decrease
      Draw rows for each tree. Draw candidate features for each split. If dollar-sign frequency is absent from a candidate list, another useful measurement can shape the tree. Combining trees helps most when the models make different mistakes across emails.
      How often does the first question change on real data?

      In a published reproduction, 100 single trees were trained on different bootstrap draws from the Spam dataset. Seventy-nine started with a dollar-sign cutoff and 21 started with exclamation-mark frequency. Even the dollar-sign cutoffs varied. Feature sampling gives other clues a chance when a strong feature keeps winning. Spambase bootstrap experiment, §9.2.4

      Does choosing fewer features always help?

      A shorter list can give each tree a different view of the data. It can also leave out a useful feature. Compare candidate-list sizes on validation data to see which works better.

      We’ve changed the rows and questions a tree can see. Now change how many questions it can ask.

      Properties of base learners

      Give each tree enough room to learn

      A useful base learner should find some signal in the emails. We also want the trees to make different mistakes, so their average can be more stable.

      When a tree is too simple

      A single split can miss a pattern that depends on two features. If the model repeatedly misses such a pattern, it is underfitting and can have high bias.

      When a tree learns its tray too well

      A deep tree can learn useful combinations, but it can also fit patterns peculiar to a few training rows. If those patterns hurt performance on new emails, we call it overfitting.

      Change the maximum depth of Tree 3

      Maximum depth caps the number of questions along a path. Change the cap and refit Tree 3 on the same 12 training draws.

      E574 was held out of training. Follow the highlighted path using its dollar-sign and exclamation-mark frequencies.

      Held-out email used to trace Tree 3
      EmailDollar-sign frequencyExclamation-mark frequencyGround truth

      What can a second question learn?

      Depth 0 makes one prediction for all emails. At depth 2 the second question can differ depending on the first answer. A tree might examine exclamation marks only in emails with almost no dollar signs. This is an interaction. Extra questions can also learn quirks specific to the training draw.

      What if every tree makes the same mistake?

      The ensemble repeats that mistake. Varying trees is helpful when they still learn useful patterns and their errors differ across emails.

      Hold the email fixed and train on new draws. How much does the prediction move when we use one tree or average several?

      Variance

      Why averaging steadies a prediction

      The first two trees disagreed on the same email. Their training draws changed, while the email’s dollar-sign and exclamation-mark frequencies stayed fixed. Now repeat the experiment to see how much the prediction moves.

      Model variance measures how spread out predictions for one fixed input are across training samples. A single tree can change its first question when its training rows change. Bagging averages the Spam estimates of several trees trained from the same batch.

      1. Keep the email fixed. Use the same held-out email you already traced. Its features stay fixed and its label stays out of training.
      2. Refit both models. For each batch, draw 12 rows with replacement from the teaching pool. Fit one depth-two tree directly on the batch. Then fit 25 depth-two trees on separate bootstrap samples of that batch.
      3. Compare the spread. Track the single tree’s Spam estimate and the bagged average across these batches.

      What changes if one training label changes?

      Keep the original three bootstrap trays and the held-out email fixed. Temporarily flip one label in the teaching pool. Check which trees drew that row and whether their Spam estimates change.

      A tree that drew the edited label may learn a different split or leaf proportion. A tree that skipped that row receives the same training data.

      Same email, five resampled training batches

      Work out the spread for the first two batches

      Once all five batches are visible, compare the variances. These are results for one email and five resamples of a small teaching pool. To measure whether we classify email better, compare the predictions with recorded labels across many held-out emails.

      What if the trees move together?

      Suppose one tree’s Spam estimate rises 10 percentage points from its usual value and another’s falls 10 points. The changes cancel in their average. When both rise 10 points, their average rises by 10 points too.

      One tree
      Average of trees

      Shared part Part that shrinks

      Pairwise correlation describes how much two trees’ predictions tend to move together across training runs. On this scale, 0 means their changes have no linear relationship, and 1 means they move in perfect step. The bar treats each tree as equally variable and gives every pair the same correlation.

      Start with 10 trees and correlation 0.30. Take one tree’s variance as 100%. The shared 30% stays in the average. Averaging 10 trees divides the remaining 70% by 10, leaving 7%. Together, that is 37% of one tree’s variance. Increase to 100 trees and the ratio falls to 30.7%.

      Derive the variance of the average

      Let B be the number of trees, σ² the variance of each prediction, and ρ the pairwise correlation. The variance of a sum has B variance terms and B(B − 1) ordered covariance terms. Each covariance is ρσ². Dividing by B² for the average gives

      Var(average) = [Bσ² + B(B − 1)ρσ²] / B² = σ²[ρ + (1 − ρ)/B]

      With three trees, each prediction pairs with itself once, giving three variance terms. The distinct pairs are trees 1 and 2, 1 and 3, and 2 and 3. The sum expansion counts each pair in both orders, giving six covariance terms. That is why three trees give [3σ² + 6ρσ²] / 9.

      Set correlation to 0 to see the uncorrelated case. Set it to 1 to see perfectly correlated predictions. Positive correlation leaves a shared part of the variance as the number of trees grows.

      Why sample features?

      If most trees start with dollar-sign frequency, their errors may move together. Offering a smaller candidate set sometimes brings a different useful clue into the tree. The shared part of prediction variance can shrink when the trees make less similar errors.

      Can a stable prediction still be biased?

      If a model learns that certain workplace words strongly suggest Legitimate mail, it may overestimate that class for an inbox where those words have a different meaning. Even a steady average can have a systematic error, called bias. Compare new predictions with labels from the setting you care about.

      Where do bias, variance, and noise show up in a Spam score?

      For a probability prediction, square the difference between the predicted Spam score and the recorded label, coded as 0 or 1. This is the contribution to the Brier score. Consider a numerical illustration where emails with identical measurements have a true Spam rate of 0.50. Two equally likely training draws produce estimates of 0.40 and 0.80, with mean 0.60.

      Expected squared error = bias² + prediction variance + irreducible noise.

      Bias² · 0.01

      The mean prediction is 0.60 and the true rate is 0.50. The squared gap is (0.60 − 0.50)².

      Variance · 0.04

      Both predictions are 0.20 away from their own mean of 0.60. Their average squared distance is 0.04.

      Noise · 0.25

      Identical measured inputs can still have either recorded label. Both labels are 0.50 from the true mean, so the average squared distance is 0.25.

      With an outcome independent of the training draw, these parts sum to 0.30. Averaging can shrink the variance part. A systematic prediction gap or label uncertainty can remain.

      We have traced one email and varied its training samples. Now use the complete Spambase dataset to test which approach classifies unseen email better.

      Random Forest code implementation

      Fit, tune, and evaluate a forest

      We saw how the three small trees disagreed. To learn whether combining trees actually helps, compare their predictions on many emails whose labels they never saw. The notebook runs a single tree, bagging, and a random forest on the full Spambase data.

      From 12 teaching rows to a held-out test

      The small demo trained on 12 emails and held out E574. This notebook makes a fresh train-test partition of all 4,601 historical emails. It uses 57 features, including the two you already traced. E574 is also in this run’s test set, so the notebook can follow it through the full forest.

      Open implementation notebook

      Word frequencies

      48 columns. For example, the percentage of words that are free or remove.

      Character frequencies

      6 columns. Dollar signs and exclamation marks use the same percentages as the opening example.

      Capital-letter runs

      3 columns. The average run length, the longest run, and the total length of all runs.

      1. Inspect the emails. Check features, missing values, duplicate measurements, and class counts. The email row ID lets us track the example. The 57 measurements enter the model and the recorded class is the target.
      2. Reserve a test set. Keep entire groups of identical feature vectors together so repeated measurements cannot appear on both sides. The grouped split aims for similar Spam proportions on each side.
      3. Compare three starting points. Use a single tree, a bagging classifier, and a random forest. Give all three the same input columns and data partition.
      4. Rotate the validation fold. Within the training split, use the same grouping rule for four folds. Fit on three folds, score the fourth, then rotate. Choose settings using mean validation balanced accuracy.

      The notebook uses a different split and model settings from the published Spambase benchmark. The curves here come from the notebook’s seeded run. UCI Spambase source

      Change one forest setting at a time

      Start with tree depth. Watch what happens to the score on training folds and the score on validation folds as the trees can ask more questions. Then try changing the number of trees, the feature budget, and the two limits on node size.

      Is the parent big enough to try?

      min_samples_split checks the parent before a split. A node with 10 rows qualifies at a minimum of 8. At a minimum of 11, it stays a leaf.

      Would both children be big enough?

      min_samples_leaf checks each proposed child. With a minimum of 3, a 9 | 1 split is ruled out while a 6 | 4 split clears that requirement.

      Which other settings can I change?

      criterion changes how a split is scored. max_leaf_nodes caps leaves, min_weight_fraction_leaf sets a minimum share of sample weight per leaf, and min_impurity_decrease requires a minimum weighted impurity drop. The search ranges should reflect the data size and the job the model has to do.

      Run a small grid search

      Pair two depth limits with two feature budgets. Each of the four pairings is fitted four times, once per validation fold. Use the settings from the prepared notebook.

      small_space = {'max_depth': [2, 4], 'max_features': [1, 'sqrt']}
grid_demo = GridSearchCV(
    tuning_base, small_space, cv=folds,
    scoring='balanced_accuracy', refit=False
).fit(X_train, y_train)

      Compare the mean validation scores in grid_demo.cv_results_. This demonstration stops after scoring the four combinations. The full tuning run refits the winner.

      Why balanced accuracy?

      On a hypothetical set of 90 legitimate emails and 10 spam emails, a model that always says Legitimate gets 90 out of 100 right. Its Spam recall is zero. Balanced accuracy gives the two classes equal weight by averaging their recall scores. In this example, (100% + 0%) ÷ 2 = 50%.

      We can read the effect of one setting. Next, look at how two search strategies try combinations.

      Compare the search strategies

      Hyperparameter search

      Randomized Search

      We changed one forest setting at a time. What if depth and the number of candidate features work together? With two choices for each, there are four pairings. Compare a search that tries all four with a search that can afford only two.

      Same candidates, different search budgets

      Grid search checks every pairing in the grid. Randomized search samples a fixed number of configurations. Compare them using the same candidate pool, four folds, forest seed, and balanced accuracy.

      A grid sees the best score among all pairings in its grid. A randomized search can miss it, and it can cover a much larger space when fitting every pairing is impractical. The best validation score still needs a separate test.

      Run the broader search and read the final test

      search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    RandomForestClassifier(bootstrap=True, oob_score=True, random_state=seed),
    parameter_space, n_iter=, scoring='balanced_accuracy',
    cv=folds, refit=True, random_state=seed
)
search.fit(X_train, y_train)
forest = search.best_estimator_
test_predictions = forest.predict(X_test)

      parameter_space gives the choices or distributions. The search seed replays the configuration draws. The forest seed controls randomness within a fit.

      Out-of-bag scoring

      Which trees can evaluate this email?

      Return to the 12 original teaching rows and their three bootstrap trays. Each tray skipped some emails. We can use a tree to check an email it skipped, then compare its prediction with the recorded label.

      Pick an email from the training pool

      Use the same row IDs, measured frequencies, recorded labels, and fixed trees from the earlier demo. The counts below show how often each tree drew that row.

      Times each email was drawn into each tree's bootstrap sample
      EmailDollar signs (%)Exclamation marks (%)Recorded labelTree 1Tree 2Tree 3

      A 2× means the tree trained on two copies. A zero means this email is out of bag (OOB) for that tree.

      1. Find the zeros. Choose a row. Only the trees that missed it are eligible to predict it out of bag.
      2. Read the leaves. Trace the two features through each eligible tree. Average the fractions of Spam draws in the reached leaves.
      3. Check the prediction. In this demo an average above 50% predicts Spam. An average of 50% or lower predicts Legitimate. Compare the prediction with the recorded label.
      See the samples and their learned cuts

      From one email to the OOB score

      Repeat the check for all 12 rows. Coverage counts rows that get an OOB prediction. Accuracy counts the correct predictions among those covered rows.

      Reveal all OOB predictions

      Why roughly 37%?

      With n training rows, one uniform draw misses a particular row with probability 1 − 1/n. If a tree takes m independent draws with replacement, the chance it misses that row throughout is (1 − 1/n)m. With 12 rows and 12 draws that is about 35.2%. When m equals n and n is large, the limit is e−1 ≈ 36.8%.

      When is this score useful?

      OOB gives an internal check for bootstrapped models. A tree skipping one row can still see another row with identical measurements, which is why the full notebook keeps matching vectors together for its cross-validation and final test. In scikit-learn Random Forest, OOB scoring requires bootstrap sampling.

      What if every tree saw the email?

      That email has no eligible OOB prediction. It belongs in the coverage denominator, while accuracy uses only the covered rows. The separate held-out example from the opener can use all three trees because we kept it outside the training pool altogether.

      You can now trace a tree’s answer, combine answers, and evaluate them. Finish by explaining which features earned split credit and what each setting changes.

      Interview questions

      Explain importance and tune the trade-offs

      A colleague asks which clues the spam classifier relied on and how to make its trees simpler. Go back to the three trees you traced. Credit their dollar-sign and exclamation-mark splits before comparing settings.

      How does a forest compute feature importance?

      Every draw reaches the first split. A follow-up question only affects the emails on its branch. Impurity-based feature importance gives a question more credit when it separates the labels well and reaches more rows.

      Multiply each split’s impurity decrease by the fraction of training draws that reached it. Credit the feature used at that split. Add the credits for each feature, express them as shares of that tree’s total, then average those shares across the trees.

      A splitting tree contributes zero for each feature it never uses. The ensemble average includes those zeros. Scikit-learn omits root-only trees when averaging these importances.

      Work through the numbers for these trees

      A feature with many possible cutoffs gets more chances to earn split credit. For a check on fresh data, shuffle the dollar-sign frequencies among the held-out emails, keep each email’s other information in place, and score the same forest again. The score drop measures how much the forest relied on that feature in this test. This is permutation importance.

      Five settings, five different changes

      Pick one setting. Imagine keeping the other four fixed, then say which part changes. Does it affect the training tray, the questions a tree can ask, or the number of predictions we combine?

      Why can more trees give diminishing returns?

      If several trees already tend to give the same email the same answer, another similar tree adds little new information. More trees can steady the average and also take longer to train and use. Compare how much each increase improves the validation score.

      How do depth and pruning differ?

      Maximum depth caps how many questions an email can answer while the tree grows. Pruning checks whether a branch earns its extra size by improving the separation of the labels. A larger ccp_alpha makes that size more costly, so simpler trees are favored. A simpler tree may vary less with the training sample and also miss a useful pattern.

      When does a branch earn its place?

      Compare two possible subtrees in an illustrative spam-filter example. The four-leaf subtree separates the training labels better, so it has lower weighted leaf impurity. Each extra leaf comes with a cost. Move the penalty slider and watch which subtree becomes cheaper.

      Cost = weighted leaf impurity + α × number of leaves. Weighted leaf impurity adds each leaf’s impurity multiplied by its share of training weight.

      These are two illustrative pruning candidates. Starting with a fitted tree, cost-complexity pruning considers simpler subtrees. max_depth constrains the questions while the tree grows.

      Scikit-learn pruning reference

      Recap Learn the Spam or Legitimate label from measured clues. Give each tree its own bootstrap tray of emails. For a random forest, draw a candidate feature set at each split. Combine predictions for the same new email and test the result on unseen records.
